articles.text: In last night’s meeting of Piedmont City Council, two proposals were presented that are designed to make it easier to create new housing in Piedmont. The proposals are separate, but both have been discussed and considered extensively by residents and council members. They include pre-approved design plans for affordable Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) and Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS) primarily for apartments. As city ordinances, they both must come before council and be voted on twice. Tuesday’s 5-0 vote in favor set the stage for the MOD and ADU proposals to become law at the next vote. The proposed amendments would declare Piedmont Municipal Code and the revisions to the City’s Design Guidelines are exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Both proposals were discussed by the Planning Commission in meetings in June, July, and August this year. The Commission unanimously voted to recommend both proposals to the City Council on August 14. The Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS) and new affordable Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) incentives, are the result of several years of public engagement, including workshops, in-person events, visual preference surveys, and polls. New incentive for affordable ADUs To encourage the creation of affordable ADUs, the City has developed a series of permit-ready designs appropriate to Piedmont’s built and natural environment. These designs could be submitted as-is, along with existing and proposed site plans and other materials, to receive a Planning permit, giving applicants a head start on the permitting and development process. Detailed construction and engineering plans unique to the site’s slope and soil conditions would still need to be developed for each ADU before a building permit is issued. ADUs that use the City’s pre-approved designs would be rent-restricted for 10 years. During this period, if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet “very low income” affordability thresholds for the Alameda County area set by the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development. Very low income is defined as 50% or less of the area median income (AMI). In Alameda County that amount is $49,600 for two people and the maximum rent would be $1,364 per month (roughly 1/3 of the income). Designs include: • A detached studio ADU, 500 sq. ft., shown in Tudor, Craftsman, and Spanish styles. • A detached one-bedroom ADU, 800 sq. ft., shown in Tudor, Craftsman, and Spanish styles. • A garage conversion, 484 sq. ft. The maximum height of the preapproved ADUs is 16 feet. Multifamily Objective Design Standards Under this proposal, eligible multi-family and mixed-use commercial/residential development

articles.text: Editor: It took FIFA four days to open a disciplinary investigation into Spanish FA President Luis Rubiales and another two days to suspend him for the unwanted kiss he placed on Jennifer Hermoso’s lips following Spain’s World Cup victory last weekend. Given FIFA’s long-broken moral compass, this came as no surprise to me. But the appalling messaging from FIFA’s pathetically slow and anemic response has actually been reinforced in the press, with the vast majority of news coverage referring to it as a “kiss.” Jenni Hermoso herself called it an “assault.” Read familiar? Recall when Taylor Swift was groped while taking a picture? Well, she also described it as an assault, not a grope. Jenni, and Taylor, had it right. FIFA’s response is particularly shocking as there was no ambiguity on what transpired between the two. In contrast, this occurred with cameras rolling and literally the entire world watching on the single biggest stage in international soccer competition. And while I imagine most readers at this point are nodding in agreement with disgust at what happened to this woman only minutes after the pinnacle of a lifetime accomplishment, I doubt we’ll all agree on the path forward. It is understandable and predictable for institutions such as schools and sports clubs to defer addressing these types of news events to private discussions in the home. And I can appreciate why – discussing these things in a classroom or on the pitch after practice could trigger a traumatic reaction and/or backlash from parents if messaging was unintentionally off-target. But misogyny, like racism, is structural - it’s not just a few bad apples, but instead a systemic disease that will remain unchanged absent a systemic remedy. Further, current events very much are, and should be, part of our children’s education. It made me quite sad as I discussed the week past with my 12-year old daughter, a soccer player herself, and realized she knew more about India landing on the moon than she did about what happened to Jenni Hermoso. If not now, then when will it be time to discuss these things with our children within institutions such as schools and sports clubs, and not just in private around a dinner table? It seems to me that time has long passed. –Anant Ahuja Piedmont father of four 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Ed Gilligan Will Becker (intern) Micah Temple (intern) Clea Villaluz (intern) SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: BroadwaySF welcomes conservationist icon Jane Goodall in discussion at the Golden Gate Theatre on Friday, September 15. For one night only, world-renowned ethologist, conservationist and activist Jane Goodall will be on stage to discuss her decades of work in conservation and as a pioneer in the study of chimpanzees. She began her landmark studies in Africa in 1960 and her research continues to influence scientists and environmentalists today. Goodall is an iconic activist in conservation. The Jane Goodall Institute, which she founded in 1977, is widely recognized for creating innovative conservation and development programs in Africa. Goodall’s global Roots and Shoots program also supports tens of thousands of young people in nearly 100 countries with projects that help environment preservation and animals. As a U.N. Messenger of Peace since 2002, she continues to help the United Nations focus attention on environmental issues, primarily world wildlife and their habitat. Goodall will answer audience questions at the conclusion of her talk. Tickets are available online at: https://www.broadwaysf. com/events/jane-goodall/golden-gate-theatre/calendar/. articles.text: No public vote required, per City Attorney The City of Piedmont’s revised 6th Cycle Housing Element is now open to a seven-day public comment period which ends this Friday, September 8, at 5:00 p.m. Changes are visible in the document and additions are highlighted in blue at Piedmontishome.org. Of importance is the topic of whether or not a vote must be conducted as the city of Piedmont makes plans to allow up to 587 new residences. Whether the changes amount to a change in zoning has been an ongoing question. In the 2022 city election, some candidates indicated their interpretation of the city’s charter as requiring a city-wide vote to change zoning. The City Attorney has interpreted the city charter to state that the charter does not prevent the city from adding new housing and no vote must be made. Changes are visible in the Housing Element on page 68 under the heading “4.G Clarifying the City Charter.” Pie d mont Com mu n ications Manager Echa Schneider explained that the city will conduct public education and outreach regarding what the city charter requires and what the zoning laws require. Any revisions would not alter the core of the City’s plan for accommodating 587 new homes by 2031. The Housing Element will set forth the City’s fair housing goals, policies, and programs to address the need for all housing and household types. The City intends to submit a revised Housing Element to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for review this Friday, September 8, for a 60-day review period. Comments on the revised housing element may be made by emailing PiedmontIsHome@ piedmont.ca.gov. • Size, placement, and materials for windows and outdoor spaces like balconies and decks • Location and visibility of parking areas The standards would apply only to developments in existing multifamily and mixed-use zones and do not change any existing regulations about density, height, minimum setbacks, or parking. They are intended to streamline the review process for multi-family and mixed-use housing developments that are already allowed by Piedmont’s zoning code.

articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) approved the immediate distribution of up to $90,000 from its reserve fund to Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) last week. These funds are intended to enable the addition of up to three new sections in the 10th grade at Piedmont High School, bringing impacted class sizes in line with the District’s stated goals. According to PUSD, an additional section of each English 3-4 and Modern World History has been created, with the possibility of adding a section to AP Art History. The goal was to move approximately 20 students into the new sections, which will reduce the number of students in each existing section. “It brings us great pleasure to share that Dr. Hawn’s response to the news of the grant was one of elation,” said PEF Board Chair, Tonya Antonucci. “We are truly impressed by her swift implementation of these additional resources, which will undoubtedly make a positive impact on our students and their learning environment.” In a letter to PHS parents, Principal Sukanya Goswami expressed her gratitude to PEF and explained the next steps in the process, assuring students and parents that changes to the schedule will be minimal. Any schedule changes will go into effect this week. “Additional sections allow us to reduce class sizes across multiple sections, meaning there is an improved teacher to student ratio with more opportunity for individual focus,” said Goswami. “More sections mean more learning opportunities.”
articles.title: Ed. Foundation grant helps reduce class sizes at PHS

articles.text: The Piedmont Unified School District’s budget has been a limiting factor this year, leading to a school board directive to maximize enrollment in as many classes as possible. Budget measures to contain salary expenses have impacted the learning experiences in classes including physics, chemistry, world history, art history, math, and literature. Piedmont Teacher Union president and PHS English teacher Elise Marks teaches the same number of AP Literature classes as she did last year, but this year she has twenty-three more students. At PHS a full-time teacher has five class sections; when a new section is opened, the teacher must be paid an additional 20 percent of their salary. Marks described new obstacles her 32-student classroom faces. “It’s harder for people to join in discussion and it’s easier for shy students to hang back. There’s a difference in how well teachers get to know their students individually,” said Marks, “It’s hard to see people’s faces.” The benefit of small classes has been researched and proven. In a study conducted by Frederick Mosteller Ph.D. 6,500 students were placed in class populations of either 13-17 or 22-25, and the research showed that students in smaller classes advanced 2-5 months ahead of their peers. In later years they advanced one full academic year. Marks spoke of a former California state law mandating that freshman English classes were not to exceed 20 students. The law was aimed to optimize the classroom environment for freshman students learning the essential skill of writing. Marks recalls smaller classes at the beginning of her career at PHS. “When I started, Piedmont English classes averaged 24. We [now] want below 28,” she said. The start of the current school year saw an alarmingly high attendance numbers in many AP classes. The district has since hired science teachers at PHS to teach three sections of chemistry and anatomy. A $90,000 grant by the Piedmont Education Foundation [PEF] has helped reduce class sizes. The funds from PEF have gone to paying for additional sections of sophomore English and modern world history which were especially impacted by large class sizes. With salary negotiations coming up for teachers, large class sizes will certainly be among the hot topics of debate. Clea Villaluz is a junior at Piedmont High School and an intern with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: Why AP classes at PHS are crowded

articles.text: The Great Chili Cook-off, held on Wednesday, August 20, in the Student Center at Piedmont High, had a repeat winner. Girls on Fire, the team of seniors Ruby Guzdar, Sara Broach and Jane Hempeck, repeated as two-time winners after capturing the top prize last year. A crowd of students, parents, and faculty members tasted each of the five chili entries. As the tasting crowd filed in, the reigning champions were hopeful, with their trophy from last year’s victory proudly displayed on a plaid-clothed table beside plates of cornbread. Guests at the cookoff were both taste-testers and voting judges. Everyone was given three tickets at the door to vote for their favorite chili makers. The Girls on Fire possessed a winning recipe, which includes a variety of beans and a secret chili powder. ”Most importantly,” said Guzdar, “it’s made with love.” The competitors consisted of a range of PHS community members–parents, freshmen, seniors, and faculty, with judging by their peers. Lively chatter filled the Student Center as mingling tasters gathered before Back-ToSchool night later that evening. “It’s a very fun, sort of homegrown kind of thing to do,” said PHS librarian Kathryn Levenson. Excited competitors brought their best chilis, including parents Eric Oldrin and Jason Venner’s state-award-winning chili recipe Photo by Erin Igoe The “Girls on Fire” team, Jane Hempeck (left), Sara Broach and Ruby Guzdar, won the Chili Cookoff for the second consecutive year. from Oldrin’s father. “He wrote the recipe down on his timecard,” said Oldrin, “So, it’s very nondescript. Hopefully we did it justice.” The team of freshmen under the name WDC began their cooking venture just an hour before the event, sourcing their ingredients from Mulberry’s. The firstyear students highlighted the recipe’s inclusion of sweet potatoes, the secret ingredient. As the tickets were tallied, excitement erupted from the Girls on Fire table, and the room turned to applaud the victors, the twotime champions. PHS counselor Chris Hartford’s chili, “Marik’s Minions,” won silver for second place in the evening’s fearsome battle. “I think it is [exciting] to bring the community together,” said PHS principal Sukanya Goswami, as photographers gathered for photos of the winning team. articles.text: A First Lego League Explore team kicks off their Masterpiece season. Piedmont now boasts the largest community youth robotics league in the United States, with over 530 students and 76 teams participating across grades K through 12. Organized by Piedmont Makers, the teams span all four divisions of FIRST Robotics: 44 FIRST LEGO League Explore teams (K-3rd grade), 25 FIRST LEGO League Challenge teams (4th-7th grade), 6 FIRST Tech Challenge teams (7th-12th grade), and our world championship qualifying FIRST Robotics Competition team (9th - 12th grade). The theme for this year’s season is FIRST in Show, with each challenge shining a spotlight on the role STEM plays in the arts and empowering young people to design and build a world of endless possibilities. FIRST is a global nonprofit that designs accessible, innovative programs and pursue opportunities in STEM while building self-confidence, knowledge, and life skills. Elementary School With the new school year beginning, our youngest teams in the FIRST LEGO League Explore division have been kicking off their seasons in homes and living rooms all across town. FIRST LEGO League debuted the MASTERPIECE challenge on August 1 and these teams are hard at work imagining and innovating new ways to create and communicate art across the globe. “The number of participants grew by over 60% this year, and over the last five years we’ve increased female participation from 6% to almost 40%” said Pat Holder, parent co-coordinator of FLL Explore with Scott Miller. “We have a great group of 90 committed parent volunteers that are coaching the 40+ FLL Explore teams, and most attended our Sunday morning coaches training in August.” The FLL Explore teams will conclude their season with an endof-season festival in December. FIRST LEGO League Challenge teams also have surrendered their living rooms or garages to all things LEGO. Teams build a LEGO SPIKE Prime robot and program it to solve missions on a competition table with just Technic attachments and Scratch or Python programs. In addition to the robot game, students are challenged to complete an innovation project to identify a problem and design a solution to present to adult judges. All 24 teams will first compete in a Piedmont league scrimmage on October 15 at PMS Morrison Gym. Local qualifying tournaments in November include the Piedmont Qualifier tournament on Sunday, November 5. Select teams will advance to the regional championship in January with top teams from across Northern California. “We are blown away by the enthusiasm for youth robotics across every grade. Walk onto any Piedmont school campus and you’ll see just as many kids in their robotics team t-shirts as those in sports jerseys” said parent Benjamin Stein, co-commissioner of FLL Challenge. “Because we’re a volunteer-run organization, we could never pull this off without the tremendous support of so many amazing parent coaches.” added Paul Morrison, the other co-commissioner. Middle School For our middle school and high school robotics teams, the FIRST Tech Challenge Centerstage season kicks off Saturday, September 9. Teams will raise the curtain on the power of design, creativity, and precision to create all new experiences. Piedmont teams will participate in a league scrimmage on Sunday, October 22 at the PHS Student Center. Qualifying tournaments run from November through February, with top teams advancing A rookie FLL Challenge team assembles their Mission Models on their competition table. to the regional championship in spring. Maker of the Year Ayyana Chakravartula returns for her third year coaching her son’s team: “Our team is excited ... so we can get to work on hardware design and building new features into our code.” High School Our high school FIRST Robotics Competition team, Highlander Robotics, also kicked off their season in August at the Ross Engineering Lab at Piedmont High School. For the first time the team is building an offseason robot from scratch, and it’s already off to a great start. This gives new team members the hands-on opportunity to practice a build season before the official kickoff in January. New members will get to CAD, manufacture, build, and program a brand new robot for a local off season competition. We hope to see you at the Harvest Festival on September 24th from 11-3! articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is known for taking on major projects where its more motivated members can take on planning and organizational responsibilities to undertake significant challenges that provide significant and tangible service to people in need. This fall, PCSC hopes to fund and build a tiny house for the new Richmond Tiny House Village, Farm and Garden which will serve homeless teens so they will be able to help themselves via the farm and garden. The construction of the new tiny house will provide PCSC teens and parents a way to not only learn construction skills, but gain general confidence in their ability to plan and achieve goals. The work is guided by local adults who provide oversight and teach skills, ideally to youth members that practice managing their peers. Shown here is the crew moving the floor structure to the trailer bed. Pictured are Matt Lewis (right), Rob Kelly, Ryan Parkhurst, Nate Seevak, Devon O’Shaugnessey, Frankie Broening, Claire Lichty, and Patrick Lerchi. articles.text: 5 ways to support your toddler’s language development One of the greatest joys of parenthood is watching your child experience all of life’s “firsts”- first laugh, first food, first steps, first words… After taking time to rejoice in these “firsts” and celebrate your little one’s big accomplishments, you may be left wondering “how do we keep this momentum going?” Here are five tips to help your toddler grow from “first words” to chatterbox. 1. Model, model, model At this stage, your toddler is always watching and always learning. They are a little walking sponge, soaking up everything they can gather (for better or for worse). Every interaction is an opportunity for them to hear new vocabulary, learn pragmatic skills, and make sense of the world and the words around them. You can infuse language into your child’s surroundings by labeling objects in their environment, describing the new sights, smells, tastes and experiences around them, and by narrating events/routines and giving them a “play by play.” 2. Expand on whatever your child says When your child produces a one-word utterance or short phrase, you can demonstrate how to expand their thoughts/ideas and language. For example, if your child says “doggy,” you can respond with “That’s a big dogHelp your toddler expand their vocabulary. gie” or “Yes! Doggy is barking.” It is helpful to vary the type of word you use to introduce a variety of verbs, nouns, adjectives and adverbs into your child’s lexicon. 3. Get on their level Get down on the floor, use a highchair- whatever it takes to be face-to-face with your child. When you are at eye level, it helps your child meet your gaze, watch your facial expressions and see your mouth movements. 4. Honor all attempts at communication In those early years, caregivers become excellent detectives, deciphering their child’s needs and learning their child’s own unique language. When caregivers respond to their child’s attempts at communication (words, gestures, signs), the child will feel heard and motivated to communicate more. 5. Follow your child’s lead As humans, we are motivated to engage in conversation about things that are of interest to us. It is so important to take a step back and see what your child naturally gravitates towards. Children are more likely to engage in play and communication when they are interested and the interaction is more enjoyable for all involved. Remember, children learn from exposure. The more you speak to your child and around them, the more expressive vocabulary they will learn and use. Paige Bailey is a pediatric speech language pathologist and feeding therapist. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo season got started at the Labor Day Bash tournament last weekend hosted by Irvington High in Fremont on Friday and Saturday, September 1-2. The Highlanders opened Friday with two narrow one-goal wins over Newark Memorial 10-9 and Liberty 12-11. On Saturday, Piedmont lost 14-6 to Terra Linda but defeated Mission San Jose 10-2 to finish the tournament second-place overall. It was an impressive tournament for George Stein, who scored 12 goals in the four matches. Daniel Banin also had an impressive hat trick in Piedmont’s 12-11 win over Liberty. 10-9 over Newark Memorial Piedmont ended the first quarter in a 1-1 deadlock, but Newark stormed ahead 5-2 in the second quarter. In the third quarter, George Stein scored 30 seconds into the second half, but Newark responded 15 seconds later at 5:16 after drawing a penalty in front of goal—6-3. Piedmont scored on a man-advantage of its own with 4:43 to go, but conceded right away, once again, just 12 seconds later. At that point, PHS turned things around. From there, Declan Linnane scored back-toback goals at 1:55 and following a turnover at 1:28, making it 7-6 to end the third. In the fourth, Finn Burke tied it at 7-7 just 24 seconds into the quarter. Stein then put the Highlanders ahead 8-7 with 3:18 left in the game, but Newark tied it 16 seconds later. Stein regained the lead for Piedmont at 2:41, but Newark was able to score on its next possession for a 9-9. With 1:23 left in the game, Piedmont drew a penalty but was unable to score. Then, with 31 seconds left, the Highlanders drew another exclusion penalty on Newark. With 14 seconds left I on the clock, the ball was worked to Burke, who launched in the game-winner. Final stats: Stein had four goals, two assists, and one steal. Linnane had three goals, two assists, one steal. Krumins had a goal and assist. Burke scored twice. Goalie Luke McAuliffe recorded two saves, while goalie Gus Von Metszch had one save. 12-11 over Liberty In another intense one-goal win, Piedmont ended the first quarter in a 2-2 deadlock, and trailing 4-3 at halftime. But an explosive third-quarter helped a slow comeback with back-andforth scoring. Piedmont battled to tie the match at 6-6, but Liberty scored twice to go up 8-6. Daniel Banin was able to score with just three seconds remaining with a man-advantage. Liberty scored to lead 9-7 after 45 seconds in the fourth, but PHS rallied with goals from Banin and Krumins to give the Highlanders their first lead at 10-9 with 2:54 left in the game. Liberty scored on its next possession, but PHS went up 12-10 with goals from William Krieckhaus with 1:34 left. With just 14 seconds left in the game, Banin gave PHS its insurance goal for a 12-11 victory. Final stats: Banin had three goals. Krumins and Wright scored twice. Linnane had two goals and a steal. Staff Photos Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team suffered a rough 3-0 loss to Skyline in Oakland on Thursday, August 31 by scores of 25-21, 25-13, 25-17. Skyline is the defending Oakland Athletic League champion, and reached the 2022 CIF State Division 5 regional semifinals as the No. 1 seed. “It was a very unique environment at Skyline with how hot their gym is, how low the ceiling is, and having to face a really good team with some strong hitters,” said coach Mariah Cardeñas. Piedmont looked its best in the first set, when they briefly held leads at 11-10 and 21-19. However, the Highlanders struggled with consistency throughout the night, committing several errors in all three sets. “We can’t win if we can’t be consistent,” said Cardeñas. “If we commit more errors than we have successful moments, we’re not going to be a winning team. It’s really just the unforced errors. We had 16 errors in the third set. We need to be more proactive instead of reactive.” In the first set, the two sides traded points throughout the opening. The Highlanders then took an 18-17 lead following a spike by Molly Wagener and an ace by Annika Hattan-Kutter. articles.text: Without winning a tournament he gains national media attention Former Piedmont tennis player Mackie McDonald made national news at the U.S. Open in New York last week , upsetting the world’s No. 15 ranked Felix Auger-Aliassime of Canada in four sets, 7-6 (7-5), 4-6, 6-1, 6-4 on Monday, August 28. Two days later, he lost in three sets to Borna Gojo of Croatia in the second round, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4, Such is the roller coaster life of a professional tennis player and its accompanying perils. Mackie’s world ranking is now No. 40 The media frenzy following McDonald’s win put the Piedmont-pro in the national spotlight. Following his second-round loss, the New York Times featured Mackie, highlighting his run-up to the match with Auger-Aliassime as a 28-year-old professional on the world tour. McDonald explained the repetitive nature of the professional tennis tour, going from one tournament to another. “Things can get monotonous week after week, locker room after locker room, hotel after hotel,” McDonald said. “It’s good to have those small goals or little things that drive you that make you believe that you can get better… They definitely show the glamour of the sport on TV. It is all the behind the scenes, it is the day to day and the around-theyear tournaments that we play that Photo courtesy of U.S. Open Mackie McDonald made national news after defeating No. 15 Felix Auger-Aliassime in the U.S. Open. Photo courtesy of Vanity Fair McDonald recently did a feature in Vanity Fair magazine in August. Photo courtesy of U.S. Open Mackie McDonald beat Felix Auger-Aliassime in four sets, 7-6 (7-5), 4-6, 6-1, 6-4. really get us to these moments.” Earlier last month on August 15, Vanity Fair magazine also did a feature piece on McDonald in an article about tennis stars in fashion. Against Auger-Aliassime, McDonald’s matched lasted three-and-a-half hours, including a grueling first set that went 7-6 (7-5) in Mackie’s favor. McDonald has previously described playing on hard courts – such as at the U.S. Open at Forest Hills, New York, as his strongest skill set. McDonald dropped the second set but returned with a dominant 6-1 win in the third set. In the fourth set, the two traded games until the set was tied at 3-3. Then McDonald took control by winning the fourth game as the returner and winning the fifth game on serve. McDonald is still searching for his first win above the ATP Challenger tour. He last won an ATP Challenger in Khazakstan in 2021 and reached the Citi Open Final in 2021, where he lost to Jannik Sinner. “I want to win a title so bad,” said McDonald. “I always find that each week, your opportunity each week, can be that week that can shift things, and I think that dream is what we’re all chasing.” McDonald also competed in the U.S. Open’s Men’s Doubles ladder with Andreas Mies of Germany. They won 7-6 (7-4), 6-1 in the first round on August 30, followed with a 6-4, 6-3 win over Nikola Mektic and Robin Haase on September 2, but lost 6-3, 3-6, 6-2 against third-ranked Rajeev Ram and Joe Salisbury.

articles.text: Staff Photos The “Mission Peeker” summit pole atop Mission Peak Regional Preserve marks the completion of the trail at 2,520 feet in elevation. The Mission Peak Summit is among the most popular trails of East Bay Regional Park District and considered the most frequented attraction in the City of Fremont. On any weekend, the location can become a highway of foot traffic, bikers, families, and dog walkers making their way to the Mission Peeker Summit Pole for their photo opportunity. Reports from this week indicate the iconic Mission Peeker pole was vandalized over the weekend, and was cut down by vandals using a metal saw. The “Mission Peeker” was created up in 1990 and quickly became the most photographed spot in Fremont. The peak is commemorated in the City of Fremont’s crest. The pole was created by park ranger and artist Leonard Page. Tubes noticeably stuck through the pole, were included to allow hikers to view their surroundings. An East Bay Regional Parks District spokesperson issued a statement regarding the vandalism. “We are saddened to learn about this incident in our park. Any vandalism from destruction to graffiti affects what should be a positive, happy experience for community members to enjoy open space and the many trails in our regional parks,” read the statement. The 3.1 mile hike to the 2,520- foot summit often brings in droves of patrons looking for a tough workout. At the top, you have sweeping views of the Bay Area; looking down on Fremont, Union City, Hayward, and the San Mateo Bridge. You can see San Francisco off in the distance and the hills surrounding the Peninsula. Senior hikers or beginners can find several places to stop on the way up to the 3.25 mile, 2,500’ peak. By Jonathan Comeaux The Mission Peak Summit is among the most popular trails of East Bay Regional Park District and considered the most frequented attraction in the City of Fremont. On any weekend, the location can become a highway of foot traffic, bikers, families, and dog walkers making their way to the Mission Peeker Summit Pole for their photo opportunity. Reports from this week indicate the iconic Mission Peeker pole was vandalized over the weekend, and was cut down by vandals using a metal saw. The “Mission Peeker” was created up in 1990 and quickly became the most photographed spot in Fremont. The peak is commemorated in the City of Fremont’s crest. The pole was created by park ranger and artist Leonard Page. Tubes noticeably stuck through the pole, were included to allow hikers to view their surroundings. An East Bay Regional Parks District spokesperson issued a statement regarding the vandalism. “We are saddened to learn about this incident in our park. Any vandalism from destruction to graffiti affects what should be a positive, happy experience for community members to enjoy open space and the many trails in our regional parks,” read the statement. The 3.1 mile hike to the 2,520- foot summit often brings in droves of patrons looking for a tough workout. At the top, you have sweeping views of the Bay Area; looking down on Fremont, Union City, Hayward, and the San Mateo Bridge. You can see San Francisco off in the distance and the hills surrounding the Peninsula. Senior hikers or beginners can find several places to stop on the way up to the 3.25 mile, 2,500’ peak. articles.text: B. Noel Thomas plays Lola in Kinky Boots at Berkeley Playhouse. Berkeley Playhouse opens its 2023-24 season with the Tonyaward winning musical Kinky Boots, beginning September 8. Kinky Boots protagonist Charlie Price inherits his father’s beleaguered and nearly bankrupt shoe factory. He finds inspiration in customer Lola, a provocative entertainer, who wants to purchase a pair of sturdy stilettos. An unlikely pair, Charlie and Lola find they have more in common than they initially thought. The uplifting play features music and lyrics by Cyndi Lauper and is based on the 2005 British film of the same name. It was written by Geoff Deane and Tim Firth and is inspired mostly by true events. “It’s just a heartfelt, heartwarming show about community and that’s exactly what Berkeley Playhouse is about. It’s perfect,” Director William Thomas Hodgson said. “The vision is a celebration of queerness, a community in queerness. As representative as this show has been on Broadway, on the West End, and around the world, I feel like we have our own special sauce in Berkeley. The commodity of this show, the event of this show, is radical acceptance and this love through community, this love of one’s self, and of one’s own desires even.” The cast includes B, Noel Thomas as Lola and Simon, Seth Hanson as Charlie Price, Grace Margaret Craig as Nicola, No’Eau Kahalekulu as Lauren, Danny Cozart as Don, and Maia Campbell as Pat. The musical will be performed through October 15. Performances run Friday through Sunday, and select weekday evenings, beginning September 8. Visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org/Online/default.asp to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Kinky Boots premieres Friday at Berkeley Playhouse

articles.text: An exhibition featuring over 20 pieces by local artist Bernice “Bingo” Bing (1936 - 1998) is on view now at San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum. Born in San Francisco’s Chinatown in 1936, Bing was a young artist among the city’s Beat Era art scene, creating works from the 1950’s on. Although she grew up in an orphanage and bounced between foster homes as a child, she was able to earn her B.F.A. and M.F.A. at the California School of Fine Arts, now the San Francisco Art Institute, where she studied alongside painter Elmer Bischoff and other greats. Her paintings and illustrations explore abstract expressionism and figuration as well as Zen calligraphy and Western abstraction. Bing only recently became recognized for her artworks, but was a fixture in the San Francisco arts scene until her death in 1998. Into View: Bernice Bing is the first in an ongoing series of collection exhibitions at Asian Art Museum that highlight the work of under-recognized modern artists. It will be on view through June 26. For more information, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/into-view-bernicebing/. articles.text: Unique event takes place Sept. 8-12 in Golden Gate Park The San Francisco Botanical Garden will host its annual Flower Piano Lounge beginning this Friday, September 8, in Golden Gate Park. This unique event merges botanical beauty and classical music against the backdrop of San Francisco’s most famous park. Flower Piano Lounge transforms San Francisco Botanical Garden into an alfresco concert hall where everyone and anyone is invited to play and listen. Sunset Piano, which hosts the event in partnership with the garden, places grand pianos and baby grands throughout the gardens where musicians and artists will play an eclectic range of genres, from Jazz to classical to AfroCuban. The event has enjoyed seven successful years of turn-outs. The program series kicks off with a Flower Piano Opening Night Special Event in the Botanical Garden’s Celebration Garden from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. Performances by Pablo Estigarribia, a Latin Grammy winning pianist, arranger, and composer, begins at 6 p.m. with the Sumi Lee Quartet opening. Performances follow each day and all day Friday through Tuesday. All concerts take place at 1199 9th Avenue in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. For more information, contact Golden Gate Park management by email info@ gggp.org or call (415) 661-1316. For a full list of programming, visit https://www.sfbg.org/flowerpiano.

articles.text: Visitors to Bancroft Gardens swap succulents and buds with their neighbors. The Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek is hosting a plantswap this Sunday, September 10. Bring up to 25 plants that you would like to donate and swap them for other plants brought by your neighbors and fellow gardeners. Donors may bring cuttings or surplus plants to swap with other plant lovers and leave with new plants to add to your collection. Light refreshments will be offered on-site. All plants must be disease and pest free and identified to the best of your ability. Do not bring more than five of the same plants or more than 25 plants total. Houseplants, succulents and cacti are all welcome, except for Agave americana and Mother of Millions. Donors will get an opportunity to “bid” on plants. You can place up to three stickers per plant to increase your odds of winning it, and if there are multiple bidders, organizers will pull a name at random and announce the winner. Tickets, which cost $15, are required to attend. Visit https:// www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/ event/plant-swap/ to learn more and to purchase tickets. Ruth Bancroft Gardens is located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek.
articles.title: Bancroft Gardens “plant-swap” this Sunday

articles.text: Benny Safdie (left) as Edward Teller and Cillian Murphy as J. Robert Oppenheimer in Chirstopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer Review by Chris Honoré Oppenheimer, written and directed by the prolific Christopher Nolan (The Dark Knight, Inception, Interstellar, Dunkirk), is based on the 2005 Pulitzer Prize-winning biography, American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer, written by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin. Since the film’s recent release it has garnered consistent praise and has filled theaters. Hence, with much anticipation, I stood in a long line, waiting to buy a ticket. But almost from the get-go I began to wonder why Nolan had picked Oppenheimer as the focus of this lengthy, restrained drama that, in truth, would have been better suited for the History Channel. While often referred to as a biopic, I would judge it as a character study of a complicated and brilliant man, portrayed by Cillian Murphy. It opens in 1926 when we are introduced to Oppenheimer as a young Ph.D. student who is fascinated with quantum mechanics. He seems dark, unmoored, and strangely depressive. This is illustrated in an early scene when he is shown injecting an apple with poison and leaving it on the desk of his professor, his motivation unclear. His affect is enigmatic, flat and detached, and it becomes increasingly difficult to care about him, no matter his extraordinary polymath genius and intellectual curiosity. After completing his doctorate in Europe, with an emphasis in theoretical physics, he returns to America, and is soon chosen by General Leslie Groves (Matt Damon) to be the director of what will be known as the Manhattan Project, which is a race by a cohort of scientists to build the atomic bomb before the Nazis, who have a similar program underway. He also meets and marries Kitty Puening (Emily Blunt). Theirs is not a love story, and their relationship seems distant, even brittle throughout. And as hard as it is to imagine, Oppenheimer was known to be reckless and a womanizer and we see him carrying on an affair with a much younger woman, Jean Tatlock (Florence Pugh), as demonstrated in two jarring scenes, both devoid of any real passion. It is at the beginning of act three that the narrative shifts. Germany surrenders, ending World War II in Europe; however the war with Japan continues. Japan refuses to yield and the Americans realize that they have two stark choices: invade Japan at great cost, or use the atomic bomb which is still under development and being tested. Washington chooses the latter and ultimately drops this apocalyptic weapon on the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The horrific destruction that follows transforms for Oppenheimer what was an abstract scientific problem into a reality of death and carnage, something that haunts him for the rest of his life. Because of his resulting vocal resistance to creating the hydrogen bomb (Russia has now become America’s adversary in a nuclear arms race), Oppenheimer finds himself swept up in the 1954 McCarthy anti-communist black-listing hysteria wherein his loyalty is questioned, and his top-secret clearance withdrawn. His fall from grace (he was on the cover of Time Magazine) is tragic. But though confronted with unproven accusations, his outrage seems leached from the story as he choses to cooperate with what amounts to a kangaroo court. Instead of fighting for his reputation, despite Kitty’s insistence that he not give in to their denigrating charges, he meekly testifies or remains withdrawn. But that seems consistent with his persona throughout this disappointing film. Oppenheimer. Written and directed by Christopher Nolan. Starring Cillian Murphy, Emily Blunt, Matt Damon. 3 hrs. Rated R. Released in theaters only 2023.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Oppenheimer ultimately disappoints

articles.text: Free Solo is a National Geographic documentary film, directed by award-winning filmmaker Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and shot by world-renowned photographer and mountaineer Jimmy Chin. It is a stunning and unflinching portrait of professional mountain climber Alex Honnold and focuses in the main on his obsessive preparation to fulfill a lifelong dream: climbing the face of the world-famous rock, the 3,200ft El Capitan in Yosemite National Park – without safety gear of any kind, meaning that singular line that is attached from either above or below to someone on belay and to the climber. What “free” means is that such a climb surpasses all definitions of extreme sports, existing in a realm that defies all description and enters the mystical, a silent meditation on life and of course death. Robert Oppenheimer in Chirstopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer Review by Chris Honoré Oppenheimer, written and directed by the prolific Christopher Nolan (The Dark Knight, Inception, Interstellar, Dunkirk), is based on the 2005 Pulitzer Prize-winning biography, American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer, written by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin. Since the film’s recent release it has garnered consistent praise and has filled theaters. Hence, with much anticipation, I stood in a long line, waiting to buy a ticket. But almost from the get-go I began to wonder why Nolan had picked Oppenheimer as the focus of this lengthy, restrained drama that, in truth, would have been better suited for the History Channel. While often referred to as a biopic, I would judge it as a character study of a complicated and brilliant man, portrayed by Cillian Murphy. It opens in 1926 when we are introduced to Oppenheimer as a young Ph.D. student who is fascinated with quantum mechanics. He seems dark, unmoored, and strangely depressive. This is illustrated in an early scene when he is shown injecting an apple with poison and leaving it on the desk of his professor, his motivation unclear. His affect is enigmatic, flat and detached, and it becomes increasingly difficult to care about him, no matter his extraordinary polymath genius and intellectual curiosity. After completing his doctorate in Europe, with an emphasis in theoretical physics, he returns to America, and is soon chosen by General Leslie Groves (Matt Damon) to be the director of what will be known as the Manhattan Project, which is a race by a cohort of scientists to build the atomic bomb before the Nazis, who have a similar program underway. He also meets and marries Kitty Puening (Emily Blunt). Theirs is not a love story, and their relationship seems distant, even brittle throughout. And as hard as it is to imagine, Oppenheimer was known to be reckless and a womanizer and we see him carrying on an affair with a much younger woman, Jean Tatlock (Florence Pugh), as demonstrated in two jarring scenes, both devoid of any real passion. It is at the beginning of act three that the narrative shifts. Germany surrenders, ending World War II in Europe; however the war with Japan continues. Japan refuses to yield and the Americans realize that they have two stark choices: invade Japan at great cost, or use the atomic bomb which is still under development and being tested. Washington chooses the latter and ultimately drops this apocalyptic weapon on the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The horrific destruction that follows transforms for Oppenheimer what was an abstract scientific problem into a reality of death and carnage, something that haunts him for the rest of his life. Because of his resulting vocal resistance to creating the hydrogen bomb (Russia has now become America’s adversary in a nuclear arms race), Oppenheimer finds himself swept up in the 1954 McCarthy anti-communist black-listing hysteria wherein his loyalty is questioned, and his top-secret clearance withdrawn. His fall from grace (he was on the cover of Time Magazine) is tragic. But though confronted with unproven accusations, his outrage seems leached from the story as he choses to cooperate with what amounts to a kangaroo court. Instead of fighting for his reputation, despite Kitty’s insistence that he not give in to their denigrating charges, he meekly testifies or remains withdrawn. But that seems consistent with his persona throughout this disappointing film. Oppenheimer. Written and directed by Christopher Nolan. Starring Cillian Murphy, Emily Blunt, Matt Damon. 3 hrs. articles.text: Rachel McAdams in a scene from Morning Glory Morning Glory is sweet and funny while relying on the very recognizable template of a young working girl climbing up the corporate ladder. In this case it’s Becky Fuller (Rachel McAdams), morning television producer who is filled with energy, a dimpled smile, lots of roll up your sleeves grit, and an impossible new job at IBC’s morning show, which currently is in the cellar in ratings. She convinces her skeptical boss, Jerry Barns (Jeff Goldblum), that she can pull the show out of the doldrums and nail the ratings race. All she needs is a solid anchor to join Colleen Peck (Diane Keaton), who has been doing morning “chat ‘em up” stories with aplomb and good grace. Becky discovers that an old warhorse reporter, Mike Pomeroy (Harrison Ford), is hanging around collecting a huge paycheck but doing little else. She just needs to convince him to get on board. Ah, there’s the rub. Pomeroy is angry and petulant for most of the film, saying with regularity, “no, I don’t do that.” He actually refuses to say the word, “fluffy” on air, driving Becky to terminal distraction. So, while Becky is all positive energy, a cheerleader for the show, Pomeroy is cantankerous, insisting that a news guy of his international credentials, a journalist who has been in the trenches, definitely doesn’t do cooking. Apron? Right, he doesn’t do that. The tension between Becky and Mike, as well the inherent tension between hard news and news as entertainment, could have resulted in some great moments. There is a terrific movie inside this happy meal that is trying to get out. They could have had some wonderful arguments about what has happened to news over the last two decades and how it has devolved into stories that are nonsensical, interviews that are the definition of prurient and banal, absent any real investigative edge. Banal is what Becky is after, however, if it will elevate the ratings and save her job and the show. There is no discussion of creating a robust hybrid with Pomeroy taking the lead. It’s all about kissing a frog (which is exactly what Colleen does, twice) if that’s what it takes to get people watching. So. Morning Glory skirts some contemporaneous issues and settles for a predictable romantic comedy instead: working girl makes it in the big apple and finds love along the way in the person of Adam Bennett (Patrick Wilson). The movie is light-hearted and entertaining. It could have done some heavy lifting as well. The filmmakers chose not to. Morning Glory. Directed by Roger Michell. Starring Rachel McAdams, Harrison Ford, Diane Keaton, Jeff Goldblum and Patrick Wilson. 1 hr., 59 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Film version of a comic book without the panels Spider-Man: Into the Spider-verse is a family friendly adventure-comedy, superbly animated, colorful, bold and captivating while moving at a breakneck pace. It is best-suited for kids age 10 and older. Spider-verse features a newbie teen (8th grade), Mike Morales (Shameik Moore), who is a mixed-race, Puerto Rican-African American kid from Brooklyn. He is struggling to fit into his new school, make friends, while naturally missing his old buds that he had to leave behind when his family moved. Kids will love its richly created, free-for-all wackiness. At the outset, Mike is bitten by a radioactive spider that transforms him into the classic Stan Lee comic book, TV series Spider-Man. The villain of the story is an evil-doer named Kingpin (Liev Schrieber) who has invented a monster laser that he unleashes, creating a tear in the universe and suddenly we have multiple universes, each with its own version of Spider-Man. To start with, there’s Mike; an animé Spidey, Penni Parker (Kimiko Glenn); plus Spidey noir (Nicholas Cage). There is, of course, the original Peter Parker (Jake Johnson); and not to forget Spidey Ham (John Mulvaney), and Spider-Woman Gwen (Hailee Steinfeld). The cohort decides it is up to them to join together to save the world and defeat Kingpin. And it’s at this point that things get really exciting. There are explosions, chases, and lots of stuff that ricochets with danger as situations change, as do the settings. The action transcends live action, which was the staple of the first Spider-Man features. This animated version is kinetic, with an unrelenting sense of humor. With victory over Kingpin, followed by the repair in the dimensional tear in the universe, the various Spider-men and woman can finally return to their places of origin, much to the satisfaction of Mike, who has finally mastered his superpower abilities. Spider-man: Into the Spider-Verse. Directed by Bob Persichetti. Voiced by Shameik Moore, Jake Johnson, Rooney Rothman. Animated adventure-comedy. 1 hr., 57 min. Rated PG. Released 2018. articles.text: The Liminal Perspectives art show, featuring the work of East Bay Asian American artists Michelle Yang and Paul Wang, is now open at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Gallery hours are on weekends from 11 a.m. to. 2 p.m. through September 17. Both artists probe the transitional spaces of emotional boundaries and thresholds. Michelle’s portraits explore this in human ways whereas Paul’s work looks into these ideas in nature’s patterns. Yang incorporates elements that blur the boundaries between reality and imagination. She explores her subject matter in surrealistic details with a touch of abstraction. Her color palette combines contrasting colors, transitioning between warm and cool tones, along with symbolic objects in her artwork that represent the transitional state. She experiments with visual representations of the shift between different emotional and psychological states of humans. Wang’s career in animation is led by a lifelong interest and career in anthropomorphism, which has gradually led him to the quiet spaces found in the intersections of math and art. Often this is discovered through patterns found in nature, both at infinitesimal and celestial scales. His curiosity has led him to computer generated art as well as physical expressions directly from nature. Paul Wang, artist Paul is an award-winning artist and filmmaker, with a career spanning over 30 years. Paul’s work began in animation, where he was a key contributor to animated films such as Antz, Shrek, TMNT (teenage mutant ninja turtles film) and Astro Boy. He explores the connection between nature, math, art, physics, biology, serendipity, and color which he expresses both in physical “natural” art and digital works in algorithmic and generative art. Sentience and anthropomorphism is a persistent thread in his work. Paul is interested in art in all its various forms including animation, sound and words. MICHELLE YANG, artist Michelle Yang is a contemporary portrait artist renowned for her ability to capture the essence and emotions of her subjects. With a keen eye for detail and an intuitive understanding of human emotions, she creates captivating and intimate portraits. As a child she spent hours sketching and painting, honing her skills through self-guided exploration. After high school, Michelle pursued formal art education with a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree from a prestigious art institute in Beijing, China. Her preferred medium is soft pastel, which allows her to infuse her portraits with a rich depth and vibrancy. She incorporates elements that blur the boundaries between reality and imagination. She experiments with visual representations of the emotional and psychological states of humans. articles.text: Part 68 in a biweekly series. City or town plazas are at the other end of the spectrum from the huge monumental civic squares found in large cities we reviewed last time. As mentioned previously, the small scale found in most intimate town or village plazas typically contains more interactive civic spaces composed of restaurants, shopping and some smaller government functions. Because well designed plazas directly contribute so much to the vitality and energy of smaller towns and villages, they are easy to recognize as the heart and soul of the place. It must be remembered that the quality and ultimate success of these public outdoor spaces is largely independent of the architectural styles used. Many of the fine examples we see are formed by a surrounding classical architecture treatment because they were designed long ago when these styles dominated. But the same important urban design concepts can be employed using different contemporary architectural design styles as shown in some of the adjacent examples. There exist important and even critical requirements for all Photos by Will Adams The university town of Guanajuato in central Mexico has one of the most wonderful small-town squares I have ever seen. It has everything: location, enclosure, greenery, density, focus, mixed-use activities and charm. It is formed by mostly three- story buildings and punctuated by a historic theater. As a result, it is always in use by both locals and visitors and is clearly the center of the community. It can be contrasted with the San Jose del Cabo main square also in Mexico. A small city of 130,000 population, the huge main square fronting on the church is completely out of scale, and clearly uninviting. Who wants to walk across the shade-free barren concrete expanse? The four- and five-story buildings that enclose this relatively small-town central plaza in Coimbra, Portugal provide a wonderful theater for the daily free music performances on the steps of the adjacent ornate church. Cars actually creep through these streets at designated times but the pedestrians always have priority. To the right is one of many smaller plazas in the larger city of Lisbon. Everything from paving, to monuments, to light fixtures and landscaping is important to the vitality of the place. Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03 3820 Broadway, Oakland

articles.text: New writing classes offered at Adult School If you are a writer – experienced or aspiring – Piedmont Adult School has a class for you this fall. Now is the time to tell the story you have thought about for so long. Gain valuable insights from the talented instructors, while enjoying a supportive community of writers. University Project at San Quentin State Prison. Fiction and Creative Nonfiction The popular Fiction and Creative Nonfiction Writing class is designed for beginners and experienced writers alike and will focus on the components of effective writing and strategies to maintain a writing practice. There will be short readings, writing exercises, discussions, and the opportunity to workshop. Instructor Caitlin McCarthy holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in writing, She currently teaches Literature and Language Arts at Corpus Christi School in Oakland. She is also a private writing coach and teaches writing workshops for all ages. Instructor Denise Bostrom Writing Together: A Poetry Studio In this workshop, students will write and read together, experimenting with new forms and prompts. The class will explore the poetry of everyday life through attention, exploration, and collaboration. This is a chance to try new things in a supportive environment, with time for both community and one-on-one approaches to growth as a creative artist. All levels welcome. Instructor Linda Norton is the author of Wite Out: Love and Work, a memoir with poems. Its prequel, The Public Gardens: Poems and History, was a finalist for a Los Angeles Times Book Prize. She is a former columnist-in-residence at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and has taught writing at SF State, the Emeryville Senior Center, and at the Yeats Academy of the Atlantic Technological University in Ireland. Instructor Caitlin McCarthy Family Stories and Memoir Writing Family Stories and Memoir Writing offers beginning and seasoned writers the tools to discover, reflect on, and write family stories. Using the text “The Art of Memoir” by Mary Karr, the class will cover setting, character investigation, approaches in structuring the work, and a writer’s voice. Excerpts from different memoirs will be analyzed, as students develop, revise, and workshop their stories with a goal of exploring layers in one’s work and supporting publishing goals. In the mouth, it has a medium weight, ultra-silky texture and expansive flavors, framed by delicious juiciness and a long, long finish. On August 13 the Family Winemakers of California held their second ever tasting in Oakland. It is one of my favorite wine events of the year. Many of the people pouring the wine have the same name on their nametags as the name on the wine label. There is a warmth, and yes, love for the wines that you do not find at the more “corporate” wine events. The span of different grape varietals was intriguing. Like to taste a Semillon or a Barbera? How about Tempranillo or Alicante Bouchet? Come on in, they’re all here. articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group survived high temperature on August 30, and looked forward to a short walk with some shade. Their first “one block wonder” destination was Carmel Avenue. The group went down Magnolia Avenue past the site of the new aquatics center, where progress on retaining walls was evident. Then it was up Hillside Avenue, across Oakland Avenue at the stop light, down a block, and across Carmel. Towards the end of street architect, urban designer, and Piedmont Post columnist Will Adams told the group he had recently written a column on the “contagious” landscape along Carmel. He pointed out the front yard of a home with an “Inca quality” stonework wall and drought tolerant landscaping. Will said it had inspired the homeowners next door to do a different, softer architectural treatment of their front wall. Will confessed he is the owner of the third next house, and to ‘keep up with the neighbors,” he had done front yard landscaping of his own. It was on to Blair Avenue, named after Walter Blair, the first European settler in what was to become Piedmont, and down El Cerrito Avenue to a set of stairs that took the walkers into Dracena Park. This park land was once part of the 8,000 acres Walter Blair owned and was quarried for stone starting in 1852. The material was used to pave Oakland and Piedmont streets and railways. In 1873, Blair’s crew, consisting of Chinese workers, struck water from a subterranean creek which turned the bottom of the quarry into a lake some 60 feet deep. Attempts to pump out the water failed. Tragically, over the years there were at least 12 drownings in the lake. The quarry was finally fenced and locked for more than 40 years. The lake was called “Blair’s Pond” with ducks until at least 1977. In 1976 citizens voted to create a recreational grass field by draining the pond. Around the turn of the century, the tot lot was renovated, and funds were raised to provide swings, a climbing wall, and restrooms. This work was completed in 2006. The group then walked through the park’s redwood grove, which originally was a creek bed, and now is an offleash dog path. The walkers passed under and then over Storyteller Bridge, where a plaque told them this replacement of the original Storyteller Bridge was Cole Becker’s 2014 Eagle Scout project. The group also walked parts of the pathways that loop through the park and were repaired in August to correct damage caused by last winter’s storms and normal aging. The group emerged from the park on Park Way and made their way to Waldo Avenue, a second “one block wonder.” This street was once the back of Walter Blair’s house. Waldo is now one of the most popular Piedmont streets for Halloween treat seekers. The long line of walkers crossed Highland Avenue and continued up Blair to their third “one block wonder,” Hardwick Avenue. The temperature was starting to rise, so the group passed on walking the short Langdon Court cu-de-sac, and continued to Oakland, Highland, and Craig Avenues. However, there was one more interesting item on Craig Avenue – a “secret entrance” driveway to the back of the Piedmont Community Church. Jim Kellogg led the walkers through a passageway to the church’s courtyard, which had lots of red roses and a lovely fountain. It was a cool way to finish a walk filled with wonders on a warm Piedmont morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Thirty-seven walkers were ready for a short walk last week on August 30. On hand were: Laura Goldman with K-9 best friend Vivie, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Will Adams, Allison Isaacs with K-9 best friends Lulu and Bode, Stacey Isaacs with K-9 best friend Pepe Le Pug, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Key Kewley, Karen Palmer, Woody Bailey, Joyce Bailey with K-9 best friend Lucy, Jim Kuo, Nancy Henn, Christine Calliste, Lisa Euphrat, Quincy Dong, Mike Henn, Peggy Shultz, Nava Shaham, Martin Levy, Ken Hubbert, Judy Love, Nancy Olsen, Tina Shum, Phil Witte, Stella Houston, Alan Goldhammer, Larry Olsen, Jim Kellogg, Helen Dong, Sarah Johnson, Chuck Oraftik, Ken Young, Rob Smith, Alissa Quan, and Dick Carter. The walkers were pleased to welcome first time walker Barbara Romain, and Susan Callen from Louisville, Kentucky.
